offence_severity: Life imprisonment and fine of Rs.1,000/-, in default, rigorous imprisonment for one year
physical_harm: Deceased died due to administration of poison, but the exact nature and cause of death were not conclusively established
number_of_offences: The appellant was charged under Section 302 of IPC, but the conviction was set aside as the prosecution failed to prove the necessary elements
motive: Alleged land dispute, but no concrete evidence was provided to substantiate the motive
key_evidence_accepted: The Chemical examination report of the Senior Scientific Officer, FSL (Ex. P/14) stating that the Viscera of the deceased contained Organophosphorous insecticide and Quinolphos was accepted, but the Court was cautious in concluding that these substances caused the death due to the delay in receiving the report and lack of final medical opinion.
witness_credibility: The Court noted that while all witnesses stated the same story, none had personal knowledge of the incident or the cause of the deceased's deteriorating health. The dying declaration of the deceased was considered weak and not sufficient for conviction.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 22.07.2003; Trial judgment: 09.03.2006; High Court decision: 09.02.2011; Supreme Court decision: 07.11.2023
legal_representation: Rajesh Pandey, Sr. Adv., Abishek Pandey, Mahesh Pandey, Ms. Nishi Prabha Singh, Ms. Mridula Ray Bharadwaj, Advs. for the Appellant; Ms. Asmita Singh, Gautam Narayan, Harshit Goel, Siddhant Singh, Advs. for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered on 03.11.2004; charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Section 302 IPC; High Court: Confirmed conviction; Supreme Court: Acquitted
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased had died due to administration of poison by the appellant-accused, and that the FIR delay was not fatal to the case. They emphasized the evidence of the deceased's dying declaration and the chemical examination report indicating the presence of poisonous substances in the deceased's viscera.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove the four essential elements of murder by poisoning, including motive, opportunity, possession of poison, and the cause of death. They also highlighted the significant delay in registering the FIR and questioned the reliability of the evidence.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that delay in registering an FIR is not, by itself, fatal to the prosecution's case, and that the FIR is a corroborative, not substantive, piece of evidence. The Court also emphasized the need for proof beyond reasonable doubt in cases of murder by poisoning.
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda vs. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116; Ravinder Kumar and Another Vs. State of Punjab 2001 (7) SCC 690; Thulia Kali vs. The State of Tamil Nadu 1972 (3) SCC 393; Apren Joseph alias current Kunjukunju & Ors. Vs. State of Kerela 1973 (3) SCC 114
